issues: Both Garante quotes re-fetched on docweb 10085432: FOUND. Press release dated 'Rome, 20 December 2024'; findings (unnotified March 2023 breach, training without an appropriate legal basis, transparency, no age verification, 6-month campaign on radio/TV/newspapers/Internet under art. 166(7) Privacy Code) all on the page.

Summary omits why the fine fell: the Court of Rome annulled decision 755 on jurisdiction (GDPR one-stop-shop), not on the merits. NT+ Diritto (Il Sole 24 Ore, 3 Jun 2026) reports the court held that OpenAI's sole EU establishment in Ireland, recognised by the Irish DPC on 15 February 2024, pre-dated the 2 November 2024 decision, so the case should have passed to the Irish authority; 'Il merito delle violazioni del GDPR resta non esaminato'. Leaving this out lets a reader think the training findings were rejected.
Significance calls EUR 15 million 'a record fine' - unsupported by any source and wrong for the Garante (e.g. its 2024 fine on Enel Energia was far larger). Removed.
Summary says the Garante's 'own page' records the ruling; kept, but annulment now also backed by independent reporting (ANSA, 20 Mar 2026; NT+ Diritto, 3 Jun 2026) - both --check FOUND.

fieldFixes.summary: Closing its ChatGPT inquiry with decision no. 755 of 2 November 2024, announced on 20 December 2024, the Garante fined OpenAI EUR 15 million and ordered a six-month information campaign on radio, TV, newspapers and the internet. It found OpenAI had trained ChatGPT on users' personal data without first identifying an appropriate legal basis, breached transparency duties, failed to notify a March 2023 breach and lacked age verification. In judgment no. 4153/2026, published on 18 March 2026, the Court of Rome upheld OpenAI's appeal and annulled the decision on jurisdiction rather than the merits: OpenAI had set up its sole EU establishment in Ireland before the decision was adopted, so under the GDPR's one-stop-shop the case belonged to the Irish authority. The Garante removed the decision from its site.
fieldFixes.significance: It shows both the reach and the fragility of after-the-fact enforcement: a EUR 15 million fine that covered training a model on personal data without a legal basis, annulled more than a year later over which regulator was competent - with the alleged violations never ruled on.

issues: Both blog quotes FOUND; both posts timestamped 2025-07-01; Prince's post: 'That changes today, July 1, what we're calling Content Independence Day' (FOUND); pay per crawl 'in private beta' confirmed.

Summary says flatly that Cloudflare 'changed its default to block AI crawlers unless they pay creators'. That is Prince's rhetorical framing. Cloudflare's press release the same day is more precise: the default is blocking AI crawlers that lack permission or compensation, and it applies to new domains, which are asked at sign-up whether to allow AI crawlers. Existing sites were not switched over automatically, and permission, not only payment, lifts the block. Summary tightened; press release added as a source.

fieldFixes.summary: On what it called 'Content Independence Day', Cloudflare became, in its words, the first Internet infrastructure provider to block AI crawlers accessing content 'without permission or compensation, by default': every new domain signing up is asked whether to allow AI crawlers and starts with them blocked. It also launched a private beta of 'pay per crawl', which answers an AI crawler either with content (HTTP 200) when it presents payment intent or with an HTTP 402 Payment Required response and a price.

issues: Both quotes FOUND. Comet post 'Published on Jul 9, 2025' (launched for Perplexity Max subscribers). Brave post 'Published Aug 20, 2025', research by Artem Chaikin, written with Shivan Kaul Sahib.

Summary says the injected instructions made the assistant read 'the user's email address and a one-time password from their logged-in Gmail'. Brave's demonstration read the email address from the user's Perplexity account-details page, used it to request a Perplexity OTP, read that OTP in the user's logged-in Gmail, and posted both as a reply to the Reddit comment. fieldFixes.summary: Perplexity launched Comet, a browser whose assistant carries out whole browsing sessions - booking meetings, sending email, buying things. On 20 August 2025 Brave's security team published research showing that Comet fed page content to its model without distinguishing it from the user's instructions, so hidden text on a page (in their demonstration, a Reddit comment behind a spoiler tag) could make the assistant copy the user's email address from their Perplexity account page, request a Perplexity one-time password, read it in the user's logged-in Gmail and post both back as a reply to the attacker's comment.

fieldFixes.significance: Unless the user wipes it, the agent's cookie regime is whatever each website's policy says: the person's own terms have no channel through which to travel.
